subtopic: ARRANGEMENTS WITH T.C.A. FOR TRANSPORTATION FROM THE UNITED KINGDOM

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Acting Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: ARRANGEMENTS WITH T.C.A. FOR TRANSPORTATION FROM THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to inform the house that the government has effected an arrangement with Trans-Canada Air Lines for the charter of planes to bring immigrants from the United Kingdom to Canada.
This arrangement will provide facilities for the transportation of 10,000 immigrants from the United Kingdom before the end of the present fiscal year. Initial destination on this side will be Montreal and Toronto.
In order to provide for this increased movement by air, existing Canadian immigration staffs in the United Kingdom will be further expanded. Arrangements will be made at the immigration offices to assist prospective immigrants to obtain necessary documentation and travel facilities, and specially trained officers will be available to provide full information about conditions in Canada and to assist the prospective immigrant in preparing for settlement in this country. Priority of passage will be given to persons with assured employment awaiting them in Canada.
Officers of the Labour Department will be stationed in the immigration offices to advise intending immigrants as to prospects for employment, and, when practicable, to arrange definite placement in Canadian jobs prior to the immigrant's departure from the United Kingdom.
The offices of the immigration branch in London are being transferred to more spacious
Immigration

quarters, and a new office is to be opened in Glasgow within the next ten days. A third office will be opened in Liverpool before the 1st of July, and it is hoped that an office can be established in Belfast shortly thereafter.
It has been agreed by Trans-Canada Air Lines that experienced staffs and facilities of that organization will be made available for making the necessary arrangements to schedule the dispatch of immigrants when the necessary medical and civil examinations are completed, thus permitting of every possible facility to aid the immigrant desirous of taking advantage of this mode of travel.
It is considered that the new arrangement with T.C.A., together with considerably increased steamship facilities now available as a result of government action, will go a long way towards overcoming the serious shortage of immigrant transportation from the British isles which previously existed.
In addition to the arrangements which I have just announced in connection with the transportation of immigrants by air from the United Kingdom, I am glad to be able to inform the house that the government has decided to increase from 20,000 to 30,000 the number of displaced persons, not otherwise admissible, who will be allowed to enter this country for permanent residence. As has been previously indicated, the displaced persons who are admitted to Canada under the present program will be counted against any quota that this country may eventually accept as a result of an international agreement designed to solve the displaced persons problem.
It is perhaps worth reminding the house that Canada was not only the first nonEuropean country to take independent action to admit displaced persons who are not otherwise admissible, but that this country has admitted more displaced persons, on the grounds that they were displaced persons, than all other non-European countries combined.
The United States Congress is now giving consideration to the possibility of admitting a considerable number of these people. Up to the present none have been admitted to the Lffiited States as displaced persons, although some thousands have been given entry under their national quotas.
The total number of displaced person arrivals in Canada as at the 15th of April was 15,410. This is a record of which I believe we have a right to be proud.
As has been the case from the beginning, the displaced persons who will be admitted to Canada will be very carefully screened by the Canadian teams which have been established in Europe for this purpose.

It was one of the cardinal principles of Magna Carta that the people should have a large share in the administration of criminal justice. These institutions, whether rightly or wrongly, are managed by officers of the crown and nobody can visit them except officers of the crown. speechtext: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 207, to amend the criminal code (pistols, motor vehicles, level crossings and the payment of fines).

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PISTOLS, MOTOR CARS, LEVEL CROSSINGS AND PAYMENT OF FINES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING PISTOLS, MOTOR CARS, LEVEL CROSSINGS AND PAYMENT OF FINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have waited until the sixty-ninth day of this session for the government to introduce such a bill. The marginal notes explain the various sections. The purpose of the amendments in sections 1 and 2 of the bill is to make it an offence to point, or use in a hold-up, not only an ordinary firearm but a pistol, or anything in the shape, form or size of a pistol.
The appalling fatal accidents and injuries from highway traffic and level crossings in Canada is mounting steadily and has become a public scandal. Almost every highway is coloured red with the slaughter. Nothing is done to avert these accidents as the mad race for speed goes on. Casualties from such accidents, and from drowning and fires in homes, are almost as numerous as those from the second world war in persons so killed or injured. The amendment would increase the penalty from "a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars and costs or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months" to a term of "not less than six months and not exceeding twelve months", without the option of a fine, and to "seizure and forfeiture" of the driver's car.
Section 4 deals with driving a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol or narcotics.
Section 5 deals with hit-and-run drivers, who are responsible for the most cowardly form of murder in Canada.
Section 10 provides that the jury in motor car accidents shall decide the question of fact as to whether the accused is guilty or not guilty on the evidence adduced. On the trial by jury of persons who cause death or serious

injury, it is desirable that the functions of the jury should not be curtailed or abolished. There has been much criticism of many cases of gross negligence having been taken from the jury. The jury are required to take the law to be what the judge says it is, and, owing to the many cases withdrawn by order of the judge, trial by juiy in those cases is negatived, and there are so many loopholes that many persons guilty of gross negligence get off. The increased number of accidents requires that the law should be brought up to date to meet the changing conditions, while preserving also the liberty of the subject.
Section 11 deals with the payment of fines by instalments. Many people on relief and out of work, or on part time, cannot pay their fines and have to go to jail-many of them first offenders with families, and some of them returned soldiers-which is another way of imposing imprisonment for .debt. The Summary Offenders Act of fifteen years ago in Great Britain allowed time for the payment of fines, and it has closed half the jails in Britain. I would commend this provision to the study of hon. members. Law reform is a dead letter in Canada. We are miles behind Britain in law reform.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 20, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gardiner for the second reading of Bill No. 204, to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject which is under discussion today is a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939. This act came into force after we had a long period of drought on the prairies, and I think for two reasons: first, the parliament of the day had come to recognize that some sort of assistance should be given to the prairie farmers to help them in the years when they had crop failures because of drought, hail, frost, grasshoppers or any other condition beyond their control. It came into force for an additional reason, namely, that farm organizations at that time began to be used to exert pressure on the governments of the day to enact such legislation.
It would be well at this time to examine the features of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, because on many occasions since 1939 amendments have been made to meet the needs for which the act was introduced.
I want to say at the beginning that since 1939 the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been very beneficial to many farmers in the drought areas. Those who have been responsible for the act should be complimented, but in examining the various aspects of it, and its 5849-207i
administration, I find that there are still many objectionable features in it. First, the act should apply on an individual basis; second, it should be extended in scope, and third, it should provide greater protection against crop losses. Because of the experience which the government and the farmers have had with the act as it now stands, it is recognized that it is not adequate for the purposes for which it was intended, but I do believe that we have made a beginning on something which will more nearly meet the needs of agriculture in this country.
At the present time we have no national planning for agriculture sufficient to provide stability in that field. It cannot be overemphasized at this time that measures directed to give stability to our agriculturists cannot do that unless we have national policies which will assist in maintaining stability in agriculture.
In passing I think I should mention four real reasons for having a national agricultural policy and what it should embrace. First, we should have an agricultural policy providing for maximum utilization of land; second we should have the principle of evermormal granary; third a forward price fixing policy, and, finally, a national crop insurance scheme which will provide coverage for all our crops where there is an element of risk. It is recognized by all hon. members that not only our prairie farmers who come within the confines of this act, but also other specific branches of agriculture such as our fruit growers, our vegetable growers and others do need crop protection against losses.
As I said before, the experience of the government in the past should give us a basis on which to work out a larger scheme than is provided in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. What we need is a scientific survey to introduce an insurance scheme which would be national in scope. Such an insurance scheme should be on a federal basis and under federal control assisted financially by the provinces and by the agricultural groups interested in such a plan. Such a plan should include all types of agricultural production which have an element of risk involved in production. The rates to producers should be on an actuarial basis, with federal and provincial governments paying fifty per cent of the premiums, or some other amount determined by a fact-finding commission. Rates of premiums should be regionalized to correspond with specific areas and risks involved.. Payment should in no case be higher than financial returns would have been had the crop been harvested and marketed. The
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

method of administration, of course should be under federal control, with proper local federal agencies to carry out such .a plan. Under such a plan, specialized production shoud be protected also. I refer to such branches, of agriculture as the potato growers of Prince Edward Island, the fruit growers of the. Okanagan valley, the tobacco growers of Ontario, and, of course, the wheat growers of the prairies. I am convinced, sir, that such a plan can be worked on a beneficial and economical basis.
I have calculated the administration costs of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and it amounts to approximately 3-7 per cent. I am sure that if the government would see fit to bring in a national crop insurance scheme this percentage could be lessened. It is for this reason I recommend that the government consider the advisability of setting up at once a commission to determine the feasibility of such a plan of crop insurance as I have outlined, or some alternative plan under which such protection could be provided to our producers at minimum cost. Such a plan as I have outlined is, I believe, in the national interests, would benefit the producers and would have a favourable effect on our whole economy.
When we recognize the fluctuations in income of our Canadian agriculturists it will be readily seen that there is need for such a scheme as I have outlined. Let me give an example. The net cash income of agriculture in 1918 was 1384,000,000. In 1946 it was $1,742,000,000. The low return for the wheat crop in Saskatchewan in that same period was $38,000,000; the high in 1946, $250,000,000. The fluctuation during that period is 660 per cent. Just as legitimate an argument can be made with respect to other phases of our agricultural economy. I would go farther and say that as an illustration in those later years we have had one-quarter of our working force in agriculture.
During that period that one-quarter of the Canadian labour force has received between 11 and 16 per cent of our national income. I think the time has come when we have to think in terms of the general welfare of the people of this country. If for any reason it should be thought I am asking this government for something unreasonable. I want to say that western agriculture has subsidized all classes of people in this country. I have in my hand a book put out by the Searle Grain Company in which they say that, according to their estimate, in the crop year 1946 the western farmers alone subsidized the Canadian consumer in the case of wheat to the extent of $110,000,000 in round figures; and

other instances could be mentioned in which the farmers of the west have subsidized the people of the country as a whole.
As I stated in the beginning, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as constituted at present, and as it will be constituted with the proposed amendments, will be still lacking in many features. In the first place, it still provides an arbitrary basis of administration and payment. In some instances individual farmers receive benefits though their crop yield may be well over fourteen bushels to the acre. In the administration of the P.F.A.A. I have seen farmers in one section, who had good crops, receiving the benefits while because of section 7 (a) of the act other farmers with less than fourteen bushels to the acre, and in some cases with practically no crop at all, received nothing. Therefore I say the basis should be changed so that a farmer having what might be termed a crop loss would be entitled to an award. It is also possible for farmers suffering complete crop failure to receive no payment whatever. That is a situation which I think should be rectified in the proposed amendments. Furthermore these amendments do not take into consideration the fact that farm living costs have increased. So I would suggest to the minister that when we get into committee he bring in further amendments to rectify these three injustices.
Before resuming my seat I want to repeat the three points I think should be dealt with. I strongly urge that the act be amended to provide, first, that the maximum amount payable under the act should be $1,000; second, that payment should be on an individual basis, and third, that the act should be widened in scope to include all agriculture in Canada.
Mr. RENE N. JUTRAS (Proveneher): Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the remarks made the other day and this afternoon on this subject. I am afraid, however, I shall have to depart somewhat from the path that has been followed by those who so far have participated in the debate.
In the first place I think I owe it to my constituents to point out that there is very considerable urgency about the adoption of these amendments. I had hoped this would not evolve into a full scale debate on agriculture as a whole, and I hope we shall be able to pass these amendments very shortly, because I know personally of at least 150 farmers who are awaiting their cheques in order to buy their seed; and at this time of year, as you know, that becomes a very urgent matter.
These amendments more or less carry into effect the recommendations made by the committee last year. At that time we thought

there was enough power in the act to have our recommendations put into operation without the need for amendments, but apparently the scope of the act was not sufficiently wide, so it is necessary to have these amendments before those recommendations can be carried out. For that reason I am very grateful to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who, having given us the assurance that he would carry out the recommendations, now has brought in these amendments. This means a great deal to the people of my constituency, because they have to do in large measure with the river lots and settlements, and the great difficulty we have had ever since this act has been in operation. I intend to go further into this question in the committee stage, but I do want to commend the minister for having brought in these amendments at this time.
I should like to take exception to some of the remarks made by previous speakers. With the possible exception of one hon. gentleman they have all made the statement that this act has been of great benefit to the western provinces. They should have said it has been of great benefit to two of the western provinces; because as far as Manitoba is concerned, instead of having been a great benefit the assistance given to that province under this act has been so small in proportion to the contributions the farmers have had to make to the fund that it has become a direct burden instead of a great benefit. If you review the statistics, the contributions and the amounts that have been paid out, I think the figures will confirm my statement. Two years ago I said that I did not think we in Manitoba could expect this act to be of any great benefit to us as it was written and being administered at that time. I repeated that statement last year, and the experience since then has only strengthened my belief.
One of the first demands to be made by those who have spoken so far is that this act should be operated on an individual basis. In other words everyone has argued that this legislation should be converted into a crop insurance scheme. In the past I have taken the stand that we should have a crop insurance plan; but to argue that this legislation should be converted into such a scheme I think is barking up the wrong tree. This has never been a crop insurance scheme, and was never meant to be such. We would have to change the act entirely to make it so. Furthermore I think everyone realizes that we would run into constitutional difficulties. I am not a lawyer, but no doubt some of our legal friends will speak in this debate, and I fear that any crop insurance scheme would fall within provincial jurisdiction.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
The moment we would start to apply this act on an individual basis I feel we would have to change the contribution, which would have to be on a larger scale. In that event you could not possibly expect the farmers of southern Manitoba, for instance, to make the same contribution to the fund as the farmers of Weyburn or the farmers of the Souris area. The various districts of the provinces would have to be zoned, and naturally the rate in the Souris district would have to be much higher than the rate in southern Manitoba, or the rate in Weyburn, or in some other areas. In other words there would have to be different rates, as there are in all insurance schemes, because in certain parts the risk is much greater than in others. Therefore that raises an altogether different question.

1.	The plan would have to be preceded by a very intensive educational program to accustom farmers to the idea of such low protection and high rates.

If one farmer, assured of 7 bushels per acre, manages to achieve a 7 bushels per acre yield in a poor year by very efficient farming, and his neighbour, as a result of less efficiency, secures a yield of 3 or 4 bushels per acre, the fairness of paying the second farmer sufficient to bring his returns to the equal of the first may well be doubted. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at once that I am in full agreement with the spirit of this legislation which, as I see it, is designed to take care of a particular situation. The basic underlying principle is logical and practical. It can do and has done the job in the most direct and economical way. In a year of crop failure when the farmer has no other return this assistance has enabled him to carry on his farming operations. It takes the place of the old form of relief which was given the individual by the municipality, the province or the federal government, and I am glad that the government has seen fit to take over this responsibility. Climatic conditions, over which the farmer has no control, may bring loss over wide areas almost to the extent of a national calamity.
I am strongly in favour of a contributory form of self-help; and I would be in favour of a contribution larger than one per cent in order that the return to the individual might be increased beyond the present $2.50 per acre, which will not take care of seed and living expenses.
I have lived for thirty-six years in a part of the country to which this act has been applicable from time to time, and I know something about its practical application. As it is administered at the present time, the spirit and intention of the original act are not carried out, and as a result hardship is imposed upon certain individuals. In dry years we may have what they call local showers, which will take in anything from a half-section to six sections or more. One point might even have a soaker, while half a mile away there might be only a light sprinkle. A streak of rain can act very much as a hailstorm sometimes does. As I see it, the only fair way to administer this act is on an individual basis. I would say the inspection would not cost any more, since every section and every farmer are now checked and a settlement made on the basis of the present legislation.
Let me give the minister an actual illustration of what takes place. Let us say that in a given township the full bonus of S2.50 per acre is paid. The township directly below does not get the $2.50. Why? Well, because sections 35, 34, 27, 22, 15, 10, 9 and 3 had one of those local showers, and in some of those sections they had as much as sixteen bushels to the acre. In the same township the sections on the east side, sections 25, 24, 13, 12, 11, 2 and 1, averaged only three bushels to the acre. On the west side of that same township there were sections 17, 18, 30, 31,

29 and 32, which did not get their seed back. That brought a real hardship on those men. As I see it, this act was designed to take in and take care of men who had a complete crop failure. The only opposition I have encountered with regard to reducing the sections from nine was because it would cost more money to operate the act in that way. I would ask the minister this question. Why chisel on this? \Miy make regulations that would cause a real hardship and, just by those regulations, exclude those men who had crop failures? There is no other reason.

I am glad the minister made that interjection, because maybe I did not make myself clear.
Those men paid for this protection. They paid all they were asked to pay. The minister knows the practical side of this whole thing. He knows that, since this act came into force, getting relief or seed is just out of the question. A man is out of luck who is in those parts excluded from this act. He cannot go to his municipality. If he himself cannot finance, he suffers by it, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) so well pointed out.
It has been said in the past that the reason the number of sections was not reduced from nine, or a quarter, was the existence of submarginal land. After thirty-six years of farming there, settlers on the submarginal land are fairly well eliminated. They are not there any more. I would say that is not a factor in this matter now. What I would call submarginal land is land that has four inches or less of top soil. I would say that land with lour inches and above-six inches or eight inches-can be farmed and is profitable wheat land today under the present advanced method of tillage and the improved grain we grow on it.	.
Further, the minister should give serious consideration to getting this down on an individual basis because that, as I see it, is the purpose and intention of the act. It was to eliminate direct relief and all this rigmarole with regard to seed and relief that went on, as hon. members know, from the individual
to the municipality, to the provincial government and on to the federal government. I hope the minister will give his consideration to whether it is logical, practical and equitable. I cannot see that it is an equitable and just method which excludes one man who has suffered under the same conditions as the man who gets $2.50 per acre.
In some cases it is even worse than that. I have seen an instance where a township has been under the full bonus, and possibly immediately south-or even north or on either side, or even taken in a circle-there is a group of four, five, six or eight sections that would not be. They would be completely out of it, just because the balance of that township probably averaged up to over twelve bushels an acre. The minister is a man who is practical enough to know these things. He has been on a farm. He knows the condition. In fact I think he knows very well the place where I myself am situated, and knows that what I am saying is near the truth and contains practical suggestions. I would ask him to consider this matter seriously, and to place it on an individual basis or on a much smaller basis than nine sections. I would ask that it be not restricted to a rectangle or square, but take in, say three, four, or five sections, no matter in what direction you go. I hope the minister will take that into consideration:.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. C. MILLER (Portage la Prairie):
subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
It is not my intention today, Mr. Speaker, to repeat at any great length anything that has gone before. With much that has been said I am, of course, in agreement, because some of the problems mentioned by other speakers are the problems of my own constituency. On the other hand, quite a bit has been said, even by hon. members from my own province, with which I cannot wholly agree. For instance, I question whether it is practicable for the provinces as such to take over a system of crop insurance. After all, if there were any great crop failure that was province-wide, half province-wide or even of substantial proportions in any province, it might test severely the financial resources of the provinces were they standing behind a system of crop insurance. I think a province should be leery about stepping into this picture, and I think the experience will be that the provinces will probably be leery of participating in any such, scheme.
Then, with regard to the administration of it, if there were to be any contributory payments or deductions from farmers' grain, if the province were handling it, it would be impractical for the province to collect.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
So far as the amendments are concerned, there is not a great deal with which we can quarrel. There are some things about which I should like to ask some questions when we get into committee of the whole, as no doubt will be the case with other hon. members. I have one suggestion I should like to make to the minister if he would turn to the bill.
I know that we are not supposed to refer to the sections at this stage, but it seems to me that there is a misprint in one of the sections in the minister's amendments; I refer to the new section 7(b). Just in order that we may be able to size up what it means, I wonder if the minister would look at it and see if it should not read "within an ineligible township", instead of "within an eligible township", in the second line of subparagraph (b) of section 7. That is in section 3 of the amending bill. It looks as though it should be "ineligible."

speechtext: It is a misprint.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
The provision respecting river lots is of importance to two or three of us from my province, including the hon. member for Proveneher (Mr. Jutras). I, for one, am glad to see them included, although the manner of their inclusion may be subject to some criticism, since the procedure to include is to be set out later by order in council.
In fairness I believe I should express my views as to the possibility of Manitoba retiring from the scheme. I know that among many farmers the deduction of one per cent is not popular, and particularly is this true in good crop areas, such as the one I have the privilege to represent. On the other hand it seems to me that this is fair and cheap insurance in our crop areas. It would require only one complete failure for most of these men to get their money back. After all, all of us have carried fire insurance, and I know of no one who objects to the fact that he has not had to cash in on the amounts he has paid in as fire insurance premiums. Those of us who have had fire insurance are grateful that we have not had to cash in on our policies.
I believe that, to some extent, farmers would look at this matter in the same way, and would consider that perhaps that is the failway of looking at it. I would not be in a hurry to counsel Manitoba farmers to withdraw from the scheme, because the time may come when a catastrophe might befall us; and only one would be required for many of our farmers to get back a good deal more than they have paid in. The surplus of $2,000,000, the

amount we have paid in more than we have received, would not last long in the event of widespread catastrophe in my native province. We have the resources of the dominion government behind this scheme; we have more than the contributions made by the farmers in the form of their one per cent deduction. If there were such a catastrophe, regardless of the amounts by way of contributions which had been made, and regardless of the amount of money the government might have on hand from the scheme, the resources of the dominion would be behind the payments to be made to the farmers of Manitoba by way of compensation, within the provisions of the act.
That is the way I put it. Regardless of what other members from my province may say, I am not yet ready to counsel farmers, if they were to ask my counsel, to withdraw from this scheme. So far as I am personally concerned, so long as the scheme is fairly administered and so long as the funds paid into the government are honestly and fairly distributed, according to the spirit of the law, I for one do not think we can have any great objection to it; because we know not what year disaster may hit those of us who come from good farming areas, just as it has hit other areas which have not been so fortunate. We should be careful in suggesting the breaking up of the scheme until we are convinced that it is not fairly and honestly administered, or that it is not doing a good job.
I do believe, however, that the minister will have to give consideration to the insistent demands that the minimum area be cut down. I do not know whether the minister and his counsellors are adamant in their determination to retain the present area as the unit for the payment of losses. I know, of course, that the minister is fully conscious of the objections coming from all corners of the country where this act applies, relating to the restriction which states that it must be a township loss. It seems to me that that could be cut down.
I have argued before in the house that it should be cut down to an individual basis, and I do not yet see why that could not be done. The minister has not said that it would be financially impossible. He has not given any reason, more than to point out administrative difficulties, which would convince me that it could not be done. However, even if I am ' wrong in my argument that it should be on an individual basis, I still believe that it could be cut to an area much smaller than a township. It seems to me that if we were to adopt the quarter township as a unit much of the dissatisfaction now emanating from the area from which I come would be eliminated.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
We do not often have to claim under this act, although we did have a little trouble from flooding in one of the areas during the past year. Unfortunately most of the farmers affected were not well to do, because the flooding occurred in an area where the land is not quite as good. The result was that the flooding caused considerable suffering. There was not a sufficient area in either of the townships affected by the flooding to qualify those men for relief under the act, in spite of the fact that they had been paying their one per cent deduction, as had other farmers.
It seemed to me a pity that those people could not participate in the fund. If a smaller acreage had been required they would have participated. I believe that much of the dissatisfaction with the act is in its administration, and that a great measure of the faulty administration lies in the fact that the unit of crop failure fixed at the township level is considerably too large.
In view of the generality of this criticism, coming from all parts of the country, although I am sure the minister has had this matter drummed into his ears year after year, I suggest that once again he should give serious consideration to the matter, and accept perhaps the quarter township unit for a trial period.
I know of no difficulty which would arise in our area in that respect. It is possible that under this condition the cost might be too great, in view of the fact that farther west they may have many areas which would be entitled to make claims, thereby running the cost up to too high a figure.
May I state further to the minister that I do not believe the farmers of Manitoba who have paid into this scheme will ask to leave it, just because they are paying this one per cent. I believe, however, that if, as has been suggested by some hon. members, and particularly those to my left, the rate of contribution were increased, nothing could stop an insistent demand from the farmers of Manitoba to have that province excluded from the scheme, and that our farmers would have to work out some other method of meeting this situation.
As it stands today, however, it seems highly improbable to me that, with the reasonably good crops we have on the average, any farmer would want to withdraw simply because of the one per cent deduction. After all, these various schemes for the benefit of farmers in general can exist only if the farmers themselves co-operate and are prepared to do their share, not only when they are going to benefit but
also to carry out the general nature of the scheme. Perhaps they would benefit from one scheme and not from another. I believe I know the farmers in our western country pretty well, and I cannot believe that they would object to this one per cent deduction when they realize that, after all, it is a measure of cheap insurance, particularly, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said, because the fund does not really carry itself.
There were some other things I had intended to say but, with one exception, they have been said. The one remaining has been dealt with partly at least by the hon. member for Lake Centre. As hon. members know, I have always opposed too much power by regulation; and too much liberty or right to make regulations is vested under this act in bodies other than parliament. I am not taking general objection to them, but I believe that no body except this house should have the power to make a regulation changing the definition of the person or persons entitled to receive benefits under this act. It should not be very difficult to define those who should receive benefits. Section 6(f) is the section which gives the power to make regulations, and paragraph (f) reads:
. . . and excluding from the operation of this act persons who, in such circumstances and under such conditions as are prescribed in such regulations, have occupations in addition to farming or do not reside on farms.
I maintain that this act should define who is entitled to benefits under the act, and I contend that no body other than this house should have the power to change that. I ask the minister to consider bringing in an amendment to satisfy us on that score.
I want to go farther than the hon. member for Lake Centre went and say again that there should be no power in any body to make regulations that would change the definition of "farmer" in the act. The government can suggest whatever definition they think will be acceptable to the house, but once that is done, there should be no power to make any change.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think a good deal of valuable information has been provided by this debate. It shows that, while hon. members are agreed about many things, there are still some differences. I was interested in hearing the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) say he would be prepared to support the withdrawal of Manitoba from the act. I can well understand that the people in that province feel that they have received relatively small benefits from the act as compared with the people in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

However I think there are one or two things the hon. member overlooked. In the last few years prices of grains have increased considerably and consequently the revenue derived from the one per cent deduction is much higher. I think that would account in large measure for the fact that in 1939, 1940 and 1941 Manitoba received more by way of benefits than was paid in by way of deductions.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext: The point I was making was that in those years the payments were made on the basis of twelve bushels to the acre, whereas it has not been twelve bushels to the acre since.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
That is a good point and I think it bears out what I have been saying. If we reach the time again when prices of grains go down, not only will the collections be less but the need for this act will be greater. I think there has been a lot of loose talk about the so-called submarginal areas and those areas which are most subject to crop failures.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated that in Saskatchewan there were 173 townships which had received benefits for seven consecutive years. He will correct me if the figure I give is not accurate. I would point out that in Saskatchewan there are twenty-eight municipalities or 252 townships which have averaged crops of between 8-1 and 10 bushels of wheat per acre from 1918 to 1943. I do not think that area is submarginal. Over a period of years those farmers with proper agricultural practices have been able to make a living.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext: There was no suggestion of that kind.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
I realize that. I am just pointing out that when the benefits are paid on the basis of eight bushels down, or in some years on eight to twelve bushels, those areas which have a lower long-time yield get more in the way of benefits than those which have higher yields. I believe that any province should be careful before deciding to withdraw from this act. We do not know how long it will be, although we hope it will be many years, before grain prices fall. We do know that in the last four years there have been widespread crop failures. I believe that if we get continuing crop failures and if prices should fall, then even the province of Manitoba could not carry a scheme such as this.
Reference was made previously in the debate to the recommendations of the Saskatchewan reconstruction council in connection with crop insurance. A study was made by Mr. R. E.

Motherwell, B.S.A., who happens to be the grandson of the late W. R. Motherwell. In my opinion he prepared a most excellent brief. While I do not agree with all his conclusions, I certainly agree with many of them. I would point out that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough) did not suggest crop failure insurance on an actuarial basis but rather on a basis of a fifty per cent contribution by the farmers and fifty per cent by the federal government.
Mr. Motherwell made an extensive survey of the results from crop insurance schemes in the United States which were based on individual farm yields. It was hoped that over a long period of years each farmer would pay in premiums approximately the amount he received in benefits, but the schemes did not work out very well. Mr. Motherwell summarizes as follows:
1.	Completely self-carrying crop insurance has not been successfully achieved for small grains in any country.
2.	Of all ventures in the field of crop insurance, the American experiment is the most noteworthy. This experiment showed several things.
(a)	That farmers in high risk areas were unable to pay the premiums necessary for their own protection.
(b)	That participation in high risk areas consistently decreased, even though general participation throughout the country increased.
(c)	That, especially in high risk areas, when a relatively large premium was subtracted from the indemnity receivable by the farmer after loss of crop, the payment was no more than a disaster preventive.
(d)	That unless a plan of insurance is compulsory, farmers will not participate in years of favourable crop prospects.
I have read those sections, Mr. Speaker, because I do not think a scheme of crop failure insurance on a self-carrying basis is satisfactory or can be put into practical effect.
Benefits have accrued from the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. It has been a help to those farmers who at various times have suffered a crop failure. It is also true that this is to a large extent a bonus, in that, of the sum of 873,000,000 in benefits which have been paid since the act was first implemented, $45,000,000 was paid from the federal treasury and approximately $28,000,000 collected from the one per cent levy.
The criticisms of the act have been pretty well covered by other speakers this afternoon. One of the most important is the criticism that the amount paid is too low. In 1939 the value of crops was low compared with their value today, but still the benefits under the act remain approximately the same, and the deductions remain the same. During that period costs of farming have increased tremendously, so that the financial difficulties of surviving a

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
depression or a crop failure have materially increased. The likelihood now is that smaller contributions will be made from the federal treasury because of the increased price of grain. I suggest that the same ratio as between deductions and the price of grain should remain. If that were done, certainly the benefits would be increased twofold or perhaps more.
It has been well pointed out that payment on the present basis of a township or on the basis of a quarter township contiguous to an eligible township results in grave injustice and real hardship. Many farmers find, when they have a crop failure through no fault of their own, that merely because they are not in the quarter township block which is placed under the bonus they have to suffer in comparison with a neighbouring farmer, even though their yield may be as low as his or even lower. The government should attempt payments on the basis of the individual farm. No doubt there would be administrative difficulties in doing that, but that should not prevent the government from going ahead and trying out the scheme on an individual basis to see whether it is practicable or not. Certainly the one-quarter township basis and the township basis as provided in the act fall short of being adequate to meet the situation.
Many of the regulations cause the farmers a good deal of hardship. If the regulations I have are up to date-I do not say they are, but if they are not the minister will correct me-a farmer to be deemed a farmer under the act must be an owner or tenant of a farm from May 1 to November I in any one year. If he resides on his farm and finds in July that he has a crop failure and leaves the farm to take employment elsewhere he has great difficulty in obtaining the bonus.
Another regulation provides that the farmer must live on the farm and have farming as his primary occupation, or that he must live not more than twenty miles away from the farm and have no other occupation than farming. I do not see why that twenty-mile limit is in there at all.

speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was not in when I told the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) that this regulation is being changed.

speechtext: In what way?

speechtext: To remove the twenty-mile limit and some other objectionable features.

The limit is the area. It must be persons who live in what is known
as the area; that is, the three western provinces. If a person lives in the United States or anywhere outside the area he does not draw the bonus.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
I would not ask that a man be allowed to live in the United States and draw the bonus. If a farmer lives in a town and is a permanent resident in the town and takes on another occupation than farming during his spare time he is ineligible for the bonus. Many cases have been brought to my attention of men with large families, who, owning one or two quarters of land, moved to town in order to have their children educated and have the convenience of medical attention, and who, because their farm was a small unit, accepted another occupation at various periods of the year, and as a result of thus trying to make an adequate living were discriminated against and declared ineligible for the crop failure bonus. I believe that an enterprising individual who has his own farm and equipment and who in his spare time accepts some other useful work in town should not be barred from receiving payment.
Another suggestion made by members of this group is that payments be arranged on a zone basis. If that were done it would remove the complaint of farmers in the province of Manitoba that they are not receiving sufficient benefits under the act. There are broad soil zones through the prairie provinces where farming conditions are relatively similar; I think the soil zones could form a basis under the act for collections and payments that would be fair to all.
I would go a step farther and advocate that the benefits of the act be extended to other parts of Canada, especially to specialized crop sections, such as the tobacco and fruit-growing areas of Ontario and the fruit-growing areas of the maritimes and British Columbia, so that the producers in these areas would receive some benefit when they experienced crop failure.
In addition, the benefits should be increased especially in view of the high costs of production. In view of those costs, a maximum payment of $6 an acre on the present acreage basis would not be too high. I do not think the farmers themselves would object if it were necessary to increase the present deductions.
The government should also take steps to have payments made on an individual basis or something approaching that. Because I think these changes should be made, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny):
That Bill No. 204 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give further consideration to extending the provisions of the
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

Prairie Farm Assistance Act to other specialized crop areas, also that the benefits under the act should be increased, and that steps should be taken toward the making of awards on an individual farm basis.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that kind of motion is provided for in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms; that it is not an effort to kill the bill, but that it is merely a resolution stating that in the opinion of this house certain things should be done. We also in this group support the changes which are being made in the act at this time.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say, first of all, that when this act was brought into being in 1939 it was certainly legislation of the right kind. It has been amended on several occasions, I think in 1940, 1941, 1942 and in 1947. I remember the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) and myself asking for the amendments that are now being provided for to take care of blocks in various parts of the country. I also think the matter of providing assistance might be extended farther than it is. A quarter township might be provided for that was not necessarily contiguous to another township in the area. That might make some difference.
While I like the idea of individual assurance, I will admit that it will be difficult to administer. I have not seen my way through it to that extent yet, and I think we can go a step farther and take the quarter township if it happens to be near an area which has been declared a crop failure year.
As to the question raised by my good friend, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras),
I do not believe that the great majority of the people in Manitoba really want to be taken out of this Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I agree with the figures which he has presented.
I was very proud this afternoon of my colleague, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, who represents one of the surest and best crop producing areas in the prairie provinces. These people are not likely to have a crop failure in the particular riding that he has the honour to represent.
This is a very cheap form of crop insurance, and these people are assured of something. We do not know what the elements of nature might bestow upon our farmers in any one year, and it does mean something to these people to tide them over. I am sure the great majority of people in Manitoba do not begrudge the one per cent deduction toward that end. I want to go a step farther along these lines and say that our problems in the three prairie provinces are so much alike that we should attempt to assist one another. We

have been having a debate in this House of Commons which certainly has affected the people of the prairie provinces and of the maritime provinces to a greater degree than any other part of Canada. If we do not begin to assist one another in some of these difficult problems our undertakings will become more difficult than ever. On that basis alone I think we should be prepared to stay under this scheme and have our deductions made to assist one another in the difficulties that the three prairie provinces have so much in common, despite the fact that year after year most of the difficulties have arisen in Saskatchewan and, to a lesser degree, in Alberta and, at times, in a part of Manitoba. Therefore I would hope that nobody will press the case too far here or on our provincial government until something else is put forward to take the place of the operation of this act.
What I do want to discuss in all seriousness are the regulations. I know that this afternoon the minister said they were being amended. But I do not like the regulations being amended by order in council. Apart from my dislike, I wish to say that most of the difficulties we have had in explaining the operation of the act to the people and all the other questions that people who need assistance ask their members have to do with the regulations. The regulations were amended a year ago, and I have been asked many questions by people during the past year. Even as late as Easter when I was home I was asked questions about the regulations and I was not able to give them much information, despite the fact that I had studied this legislation closely.
The regulations are now being amended.
I make a plea to the minister that when we go into committee of the whole on this bill we be given the privilege of passing on these regulations rather than having it done by order in council. If that cannot be done I ask him to bring us up to date on the regulations and let us know as nearly as possible in detail what they are. The whole thing should be placed in detail before the committee of the whole when we are at the proper stage of this legislation.
I do not wish to take up any more time now; I shall have questions to ask when we are in committee, and I sincerely hope that the minister will agree with the suggestions I have made so that we may work in greater co-operation with the people who come under this assistance measure.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
As the
seconder of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue), I should like to say it is significant that, while the bill which is now before the

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
house is to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, 1939, in certain particulars very little of what has been said this afternoon has referred directly to the amendments proposed by this bill. This is not because hon. members do not approve these amendments. Personally I think these amendments were called for and are very much in order, but the fact that the discussion has been on a different phase of the original act itself is indicative of the need for further amendments which are not included in the present bill.
Last summer we had the advantage of having a visit in the town of Dauphin from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), a few weeks after we had a rather disastrous flood in that area. The minister will recall that at that time local officials of the municipalities concerned took advantage of his visit to address a public meeting and invited him to meet the municipal officials in order that they might place their representations before him. He will also recall that in making these representations they were unanimous in the plea that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be so amended as to make it possible for farmers to qualify for prairie farm assistance where they cannot do so under the present township plan.
I am not going to repeat the arguments I used in this house two years ago or last year in proposing certain changes in the act so as to make it more applicable in case of crop loss or damage from hail or flood. What other speakers have said today ought to be enough to persuade the Minister of Agriculture that a substantial change is required in that respect. But I do wish to impress on him the fact that the experience we have had in the part of Manitoba from which I come, shows that the farmers for many years paid their share of the prairie farm assistance fund, paid it cheerfully and without any grumbling, then were faced one year with a disastrous flood and, because of the regulations and the provisions of the act as it now stands, found that a great number of them were not able to qualify in spite of the fact that their [DOT]crops were completely washed out by the flood. One can understand that there will be a great deal of resentment and disappointment among those farmers. The figures which have been quoted today show that the farmers of Manitoba have contributed to the fund about two and a half times what they have taken out, which I think is a further argument in favour of certain changes being made in respect of the province of Manitoba.
While I am on that subject I want to make it clear, as I did two years ago, that while I respect the views of the hon. member for
Provencher (Mr. Jutras), I do not agree with his contention that Manitoba should seek to secede from this plan. Last year around Dauphin we had disaster strike a large area; and anyone coming from such a district will realize that but for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act these people would not be able to obtain assistance of any kind. It is perhaps interesting to note that, while the hon. member for Provencher made reference to the fact that a year or two ago the provincial minister of agriculture of Manitoba said that in his opinion Manitoba's contribution to the fund should be laid aside in order to build up a fund for a provincial crop insurance scheme, only a few days ago the premier of that province said that in his opinion what is required is an amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to make it more applicable to cases such as I have described.
That statement was made to a delegation consisting of several persons from around Dauphin who interviewed the Premier of Manitoba in an endeavour to obtain assistance from his government for those farmers who could not qualify under the present provisions of this legislation. It was estimated that approximately $10,000 would be required to cover those farmers who could not qualify under this act. speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, April 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rinfret for the second reading of Bill No. 8, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McCullough (Assiniboia).

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OP CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this debate has been under way for some considerable time, a matter of such great importance should in my opinion have the careful attention of members in all sections of the house. I might remind the house that it was just about twenty years ago that representations were made to parliament to increase the capital from $75,000,000 to $150 million, an increase of 100 per cent, which, in the terms of the amendment before the house, would seem to be a reasonable amount.
I am sure those who were sponsoring the legislation at that time were of the opinion that no greater increase could be warranted. Now, however, we are being asked to increase the capital from $150 million to $500 million, or an increase of 233 per cent, or about five times the increase granted in 1928.
Let me make it clear at the outset that I have no personal fault to find with the Bell Telephone Company. The service they have given me and my family while we have used it has always been of a very high order. Some of my friends have been employed by the company over a period of years, and I have never heard any criticism of their labour relations or the working conditions.
But, Mr. Speaker, this corporation is now in the monopoly category, and before parliament is asked to put its stamp of approval upon the type of legislation before us we should inquire whether the public interest is being served by this type of legislation.
When the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) was sponsoring the legislation he drew our attention to some information contained in the Canada Year Book for 1947 in connection with the telephone systems of Canada. He mentioned that there were 3,151 telephone systems in 1945. It is inter-

esting to note that, although we have 3,151 systems, one of them has over 60 per cent of the total investment in Canada, whereas the remaining 3,150 have less than 40 per cent.
When reading, the hon. member left out one significant sentence in the paragraph. I am sure no offence was intended but, to keep the record complete, I think I should place it on Hansard. That sentence is as follows:
Of the 2,368 co-operative telephone companies no few'er than 1,121 were in Saskatchewan alone, 785 in Alberta and 212 in Nova Scotia.
Hon. members might find it of interest to have the complete story of the efforts which have been made by people in various parts of Canada to provide telephone service for themselves in areas where the Bell Telephone Company was not interested in making expenditures.
For instance, in 1946 in Prince Edward Island there were 35 co-operative companies; in Nova Scotia, 214; New Brunswick, 9; Quebec. 78; Ontario, 116; Manitoba, 5; Saskatchewan, 1,106; Alberta, 788, and British Columbia 3. This makes a total of 2,354 co-operative organizations which were in the telephone business in 1946.
But the facts are that the Bell Telephone Company is a near monopoly; it controls a very large investment in Canada.
In the Financial Post survey of corporate securities for 1946, I find some information which conflicts with that which was given by the hon. member for Outremont in piloting the bill. The survey of corporate securities states that 21-7 per cent of the outstanding stock of the Bell Telephone Company is held by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.

It is one of the first times anyone has questioned publicly the accuracy of the survey of corporate securities. In view of the fact that it. is some little time since the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) first drew this matter to the attention of the house, I think the publishers of

Bell Telephone Company
this publication would have made some correction, if they had given this information incorrectly.
I have mentioned that many of the directors of the Bell Telephone Company are interested in many other large corporations in Canada. There is no law against that; but I might mention, for example, that Mr. Sise, the chairman of the board, is also a director of the Bank of Montreal. The Hon. Charles A. Dunning, whose name was mentioned in connection with the Canadian Pacific claim for increased freight rates is also a director of the Bell, a director of the Bank of Montreal and a great many other organizations the names of which I shall not take time to mention. Mr. Angus, one of the Bell directors, is a director of the Royal Bank of Canada; and so on, down the list.
There is no law against that, but I think members of the house should be cognizant of the fact that we are being asked to give special privileges to a near monopoly which apparently is in a field where we should have public ownership. I notice that in 1928 the same objections were made as are being made during this debate. It is unfortunate that in the passing of twenty years so few of those who took part in an important debate are spared to carry on, but it is interesting to note that the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) were here in 1928. They expressed their views effectively at that time as well as on this occasion. I was interested in reading the comments made by the then member for Mackenzie, Mr. Milton Campbell. On page 3089 of Hansard of May 16, 1928 we find a record of his speech. He quoted from a brief which had been presented on behalf of the province of Ontario as follows:
What a public scandal this is, to have the same directors sitting on the board of the Bell Telephone Company and also on the board of the Northern Electric Company, buying from and selling to themselves, with the assistance of Western Electric Company directors, and fixing the prices among themselves that the poor milch cow, the Bell Telephone Company, shall pay for such apparatus, equipment and supplies. Is it any -wonder the treasury of the Bell is depleted systematically when any money appears, and the contents pipe-lined over to the treasury of the Northern Electric and ultimately into the treasury of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. As a glaring instance of this, let me illustrate by citing the annual dividend payment of eight per cent and two per cent bonus, or about ten per cent paid by the Northern to the Bell, on the latter's share holdings in the former, amounting to $3,900,000. The dividend payment would be about $300,000. This amount is no sooner paid to the Bell than it is sluiced across the international boundary line and into the treasury of the American company as a payment under the 1923 service contract.
Mr. Campbell also complained about the fact that the telephone companies in the prairie provinces were obliged to buy the major part of their equipment from Northern Electric at prices fixed by a company controlled by Bell. According to the Financial Post "Survey of corporate securities", the Bell Telephone has the following subsidiaries: Kamouraska Telephone Company Ingersoll Telephone Company-North America Telegraph Company The Southern Ontario Telephone Company-Limited
Woodbridge and Vaughan Telephone Company Limited
Canadian Telephone Company
C'hapleau Telephone System
Charlevoix and Saguenay Telephone Company
Welland County Telephone Company
Labelle Telephone Company
Yamaska Telephone Company
New Brunswick Telephone Company
It is unfortunate that this whole matter could not be referred to a committee so that we could hear the officers of the Bell Telephone Company and give them a chance to justify the set-up and give their explanations for what has been done. It is significant that no hon. members on the government side have been taking part in the debate and giving us the information to which I think we are entitled.
During his remarks the hon. member for Outremont referred to the future plans of the company affecting rural service. He is reported on page 1701 of Hansard of February 27, 1948, as saying:
The estimated increase in telephones in rural areas in the next four years depends on the company's ability to obtain material and equipment. It is expected, however, that 38,400 additional telephones will be installed and an amount of $25,600,000 spent.
It always interests me that whenever somebody wants to get something done they figure that if they shed some crocodile tears for the poor farmer in any part of Canada they will get full co-operation. I presume it was thought that if some mention were made of plans for rural service it would expedite the passage of this bill to provide an increase in capital from $150 million to $500 million. The hon. member went on to say:
At the end of 1951 it is estimated that between 65 and 70 per cent will have service in the rural areas. These figures will be very close to the development in urban areas.
I made a study of telephone service in rural areas in Canada; and I wish to draw the attention of the house to the dominion bureau of statistics housing census of Canada for 1941, dealing with automobiles, radios, telephones and vacuum cleaners in Canada. I should like to give the house the percentages of the population having telephone service in the different

Members will note that, as far as rural telephone service is concerned, Ontario places first, Saskatchewan second, Nova Scotia third, Manitoba fourth, British Columbia fifth, Alberta sixth, Prince Edward Island seventh, with New Brunswick and Quebec being tied with 16 per cent. I do not know how the hon. member for Outremont can expect members of parliament to accept the claim that by 1951 it is estimated that 65 to 70 per cent of those in rural areas will have service, when in the period from 1880, when Bell first started to function in Canada, to 1941 the best that could be accomplished was 29 per cent. In the areas which the Bell is serving in Quebec and New Brunswick the farm percentage is 16 per cent. I am sure it will be difficult to increase that ratio by 1951 from 16 or 17 per cent to 65 or 70 per cent as the hon. member for Outremont has mentioned. It is very important that people in the rural areas should have telephone service in case of sickness, when life and death may hang in the balance.
We cannot allow a bill of this kind to pass without drawing attention to the fact that the Bell Telephone Company has been chiefly concerned in going into the larger cities where the greatest amount of revenue can be got most easily. In the province where it has its head office it gives a very good service in the big cities; but, according to the 1941 statistics, in rural Quebec only sixteen farm families out of one hundred have a telephone service. The people in the rural parishes in the province of Quebec and those who work on farms in outlying areas should have this modern convenience which is regarded as almost a necessity by most people, and so I think the sponsor of the bill should have some comment to make on the plans of the company to improve its service particularly in the rural districts of Quebec and New Brunswick. In Ontario the ratio is much better, but there I understand that the Bell Telephone Company cannot claim the credit for promoting the construction of rural telephone lines.

Another passage in the speech made by the sponsor of the bill deserves careful examination. At page 1704 of Hansard he is reported
to have said:
Section 5 of the bill, which deals with wireless and radiotelephone services, is intended to clarify the company's powers under its original act of incorporation with regard to the use of the latest improvements in the art of telephony, including radio and wireless telephone and television, in providing the communication service which it furnishes. Wireless and radiotelephone is a comparatively new development in the art of communication and lies in the field in which the company operates. It is important not only to the company but to the public service which the company provides that there should be no question as to its powers to furnish service by this means.
I cannot find anywhere authorities who take it for granted that this is a field which has been assigned to the Bell Telephone Company. With the developments that are taking place in wireless and radiotelephone services, it seems to me that section 5 of the bill should not be accepted in principle. If this bill had been presented to parliament without this particular section we should not have had as interesting a debate as we have had. Those of us who are concerned about public ownership cannot accede to the handing over to a privately owned company of the monopoly to operate wireless and radiotelephone services.
Further on, he said:
Wireless telephone or radio is assuming increasing importance in the economical development of the telephone system. Developments in recent years have progressed rapidly and there is every likelihood that wireless telephone or radio systems capable of handling large numbers of communication channels over long distances may in many cases prove to be an economical alternative to the use of wire lines. Since the economical development of the company's system involves the use of such new developments as become available, it is planned to use wireless telephone and radio systems as an alternative to wire lines.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Outremont will not ask parliament to approve the principle of a bill containing such objectionable provisions.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I must not overlook to pay a tribute to my close neighbour the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who made such an outstanding contribution in the earlier stages of this debate, also the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who was able to speak as eloquently in this debate as he did twenty years ago. I am glad to be associated with these two outstanding Canadian citizens in a struggle to keep for the people the right to have public ownership in the field of communication. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the bill should not pass in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the house for only a few moments, and the effort which I shall make is an appeal to the C.C.F. to stop this filibuster. I shall be reasonable in the moderate language I use and shall make no wisecracks or smart replies. I am anxious that this house, particularly these hon. gentlemen to my left, should see just where we are going in the attitude which they have taken.
Since confederation incorporations of this kind have been made by the dominion parliament, but if the C.C.F. persist in the line which they have now taken, that power of this parliament is taken away from it completely. It will mean that a small group of people, with the limited time which we now have owing to major matters of importance which have to be discussed here, can gather themselves together and destroy a power which rests in this parliament. That is exactly what we are witnessing at the present time.
May I absolve myself immediately from any connection with the Bell Telephone Company. We do not have it where I live, and I have no acquaintance whatsoever with any officer of that company. It is spread wide in this area of Canada. A lot of figures were given just now. I speak only of the province of Alberta, but I think it is also true of the province of Saskatchewan. Alberta had a rural telephone system but it was a complete failure through lack of support. Therefore we have today in that province the farmers grouping together and forming their own organizations, maintaining their lines and so on, in order that they may have telephone service. In other words, the government of that province could not support rural telephones. Although I do not make it as an accurate statement, I think it is true of Saskatchewan also.
Two things seem to be at issue; one, the increase in capital. I have no hesitation in saying that at the moment, without knowing more than has been given to us here, it seems to me too large an increase. That is said without any complete examination of the facts. But on the run-of-mine reasons, if I may say so, that influence our minds it strikes me as a tremendous increase.
The other thing they say is that the Bell Telephone Company should have the authority in brother fields or fields of the same type of communication. I do not agree with them in that. Any company which is dealing with communications must have an eye to the future. I wonder, sir, how many hon. members in this house have read the address recently given by Mr. Frank Stanton, president of
the Columbia broadcasting system, whose acquaintance over a very good lunch I had an opportunity of making; and that is my only connection with him. He paid for it and we had a very good lunch. He visualized within the next twenty-five years, and with authority, that you would have a vest-pocket radio not larger than your watch, and you would also have a sending set not larger than your watch, with which you could communicate with your wife and tell her that you would be late for dinner, or whatever message jmu cared to send.
He also said that it is well within reason- these are not imaginings; they have gone a long way-that when you telephoned somebody you would see the person at the other end to whom you were talking. That will stop a lot of fellows calling up somebody and saying you are talking to your wife, because it may be the maid to whom you are talking or somebody else in your house. Then it is well within reason that within ten years when you get up in the morning and go to your radio you will have a newspaper in that radio in colour, folded and so on and you will have the news at your breakfast when you sit down to eat your morning meal. What company like the Bell Telephone Company should not anticipate things of that kind which are anticipated in radio and which are certainly well within reason within twenty-five years?
To hear some of my friends speak, one would think Alexander Bell was an enemy of society instead of being one of the greatest men that this world, and particularly this Canada, ever gave birth to.
Here is my point, and here is my appeal. Why not let this bill go to a committee? Cut down the capitalization if it is too high; eliminate some of the powers which are sought if they do not justly belong to this company. But let it be stopped now and never said of this parliament that a small group by a filibuster can thwart laws which we all have thought sound since 1867. Go to that committee and amend the bill in any way you wish. You can cut down the powers; you can cut down the capitalization. There you will have before you men who must justify what they are asking for.
It does not seem to me to be within the mouth of anyone to say that the sponsor of a bill of this kind should supply the House of Commons with complete explanations, authorities and plans for future operations and construction. None of us would ever sponsor a bill ini this house, unless it were something with which we had grown up, some business with which we were entirely
