subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OP CANADA
speechtext:
When this bill was called the first time for second reading I made as full and complete a statement to the house as I could. I took

every minute at my disposal in the forty minutes that I had. I might say right away to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) that the reason a private member is presenting this bill is simply that a minister cannot present a private bill. The reason I had prepared a statement at that time was to crowd in as much as I possibly could in as few words as I possibly could use. Because I spoke for forty minutes, I was congratulated by some hon. members on the other side on helping them to talk out the bill.
If one reads the introductory statement that I made he will recognize that practically every obstacle and every objection that have been made to the bill have been answered. This is a private company, first of all, and there cannot be any question of public ownership at this time. It is a private company, duly incorporated; and surely the principle of this bill is not whether or not this company can be publicly owned.
I gave a long history of the company to show that this was not a monopoly of the octopus type that my hon. friends on the other side wish it to appear. In the beginning the company had authority to cover the whole of Canada except British Columbia. In January, 1908. they relinquished the territory now comprising Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. Later they relinquished the territory taking in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. In Quebec and Ontario they have retained a certain amount of the territory, though not all. They are not a "grab-all" concern. They are a competitive monopoly carrying on business in Quebec and Ontario with 893 other companies, 578 in Ontario and 315 in Quebec. There are also thirty-three other non-connecting companies or systems.
If my hon. friends wish to call this company a monopoly in the sense used the other day by the hon. member for High Park (Mr. McMaster), when he said he could not dream of two telephone systems operating in the same area; if that is what they mean by a monopoly, I am with them and this company is a monopoly. Within its territory there is only one telephone system. But it is a monopoly that is fully and completely controlled by the board of transport commissioners. Its rates have been subject to regulation since 1892. It has been subject to all pertinent, provisions of the Railway Act and the regulatory jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners since 1906. The issue of capital stock has been subject to the jurisdiction of the board since 1929, or for the past nineteen years. No other private company in Canada is so well controlled by the board of transport commissioners.

Bell Telephone Company
Objection has been taken to the increase in capital. I submit that this is not a principle of this bill and should not have been discussed on second reading. In my statement I gave the financial position of the company at the present time. I gave details as to the intended construction and gave the estimate of the company at that time, amounting to over $700 million. I did not separate the amounts in the various years. They are as follows:
1948	 $74,000,000
1049		 76,000,000
1050		 71,000,000
1951		 71,000,000
1952		 70,000,000
For the following five years an expenditure of $68,000,000 a year is anticipated. A moment ago the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) said we were trying to make stock by appealing to the rural areas. I did not say the whole of the province of Quebec was controlled by the Bell system, but only part of it. And I said in my introductory remarks that within the Bell system area in 1945 some 39 per cent of the establishments had service. In 1947 this figure had reached 55 per cent, and it is estimated that by 1951 between 65 and 70 per cent will have service. That is within the area served by the Bell system, not the other companies. That was my statement and I repeat it.

speechtext:
Yes, in the area served by the Bell system.
In my introduction I also said I realized the increase was substantial, but that the program contemplated is also substantial. In my final remarks I said hon. members would have full opportunity in committee to examine the various questions involved.
During this discussion three suggestions have been made by hon. members who have let their imagination run wild. One was that this amount of money was to be used to purchase the provincial systems. My answer to that is an emphatic no. Another hon. member thought we might use this money to build a line through the United States to by-pass the western provinces in order to deprive them of large revenues. My answer to that is that there is no such intention. At the present time there is a line operated by the Trans-Canada telephone system, which is some sort of co-operative system in which all telephone systems including the provincial systems share
both as to revenue and as to cost of operation, and which serves as a sort of clearing house for the purpose. So there is no such intention.
Another hon. member suggested this additional capital might be used to purchase, through War Assets, a complete communication system developed during the war by the army, navy and air force. There again my answer is that there is no such intention. The new capital will be used as I have indicated, to extend the company's plant and facilities in Ontario and Quebec, and there is no intention on the part of the Bell company to invade the territory of any other system in those provinces.
Another matter brought up was the splitting of shares, and again I suggest that is not the principle of the bill. I might say to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough) that never before has the Bell company split its shares. This was imposed in the other place. It does not mean any change in the situation for the shareholders, except that out of the grand total they will have four times as many shares. The ratio will remain constant.
As far as revenue is concerned, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) spoke of ten per cent which might be reduced to two and one-half per cent. That is impossible. The percentage will remain the same; it will be eight per cent, but it will be eight per cent on S25 instead of eight per cent on $100. Since the shares are now selling at $165, however, the percentage of dividends at present is 4-65.
Someone brought up the question of radio and television. Again that is not the principle of the bill, but of only one section. The company has no intention of going into the business of broadcasting radio or television programs. It will continue, as it is doing at present, to link various programs initiated by others. It has the power, which it asks to have confirmed, to operate in the radiotelephone field. This it does under proper licence obtained from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which permits it to operate mobile telephones and the like, in order to bring service to outlying districts and in order to have it as stand-by equipment in ease of storm damage, and so on.
I dealt with all these matters in my introductory remarks. At that time I did not deal with rates, because I did not consider that matter came in on second reading. The principle of the rates is quite a complicated matter, which might be fully dealt with in committee.
One thing I should like to explain is the question of free connection. If every hon. member would take a pencil and piece of paper
Bell Telephone Company

and put two dots on the paper representing two telephones, in order to connect those telephones they will require one pair of lines. If they add one more dot, representing a third telephone, they will have to add two more lines, so that there the ratio will be one to one as against one to two as it was before. If they add another telephone, they will have to add three lines, making six lines for four telephones. If they go on to five telephones they will require ten lines, or a ratio of two to one. If they continue on to ten telephones and interconnect them they will have forty-five lines connecting the ten telephones, or a ratio of 4-5 to 1. If they go on to 10,000, which is the limit for a central office, they will require 49,995,000 lines to connect them, or a ratio of 4,999-5 to 1. That is why it is more expensive to instal telephones in large cities.
The Bell company has been said by hon. members everywhere to be a well managed and efficient company. We are told that they have a fine group of directors, who are jealous of the reputation the company has built up for service and efficiency. They wish to keep that wonderful reputation. They wish to maintain good relations with their employees, so that those employees will be able to say, as the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore) said, that this is one of the best of private companies for which an individual could wish to work.
They want to keep that reputation among their clients, and at the present time they are concerned because they cannot provide a better service than they are doing. They are concerned because there are 95,749 unsatisfied applications for service. That is an increase of 1,700 over the figure I quoted last time. There are some 69,000 reported eases of people having a party line who would like to have a single line. There are some thousands of people like myself in the country who would like to have single lines but who cannot obtain them.
In 1902, by chapter 41 of the statutes, parliament imposed upon the company the obligation of furnishing telephones on demand. They are not in a position to do so today. They ask to be put in that position. They are operating a public service and they know it. They are trustees for the public and they know it. That is why they come before parliament and they say, "We need what we are asking in this bill in order to be able to discharge our obligations to the public. We expect to be obliged to explain why we need those powers." Are we to refuse this company the opportunity to discharge its obliga-

lions? Are we to deny to people who have not a telephone today, the use of a telephone
service?
The principle of this bill-and that is the only principle which applies to the whole of this bill-is whether or not we shall authorize this company to perform its obligations toward the public. The company says it needs the provisions contained in the bill. The hon. member for High Park says that the Bell Telephone Company is all the time trying to find out what the necessities of the future will be. Then I ask hon. members to let this bill go to the committee. The committee will study it attentively. It must do so. It is its duty to do so, because it is an important bill. The committee will decide whether or not the company is entitled to obtain what it asks for.
We are on second reading of a private bill. I wish to refer hon. members to Beauchesne, third edition, notation 769. There they will see that on second reading of a private bill the situation is different from that on second reading of a public bill. The second reading of a private bill is only a conditional approval of the principle. It is conditional upon proof before the committee of the various facts that are set out in the bill. That appears in notation 769 of Beauchesne. Therefore the objection that has been made, that if we give second reading to this bill the principle will be accepted, does not hold water. The principle is accepted only conditionally. If the company cannot prove what it advances; if the experts cannot show that they need this money, then the committee is entitled to reduce the amount or to do whatever it pleases.
Everybody knew this rule, or at least everybody is supposed to know it is there. That is the rule with regard to a private bill. What are we met by? We are met by a sugar-coated six months' hoist by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), which is meaningless in the light of this notation 769. I think the purpose of the amendment was just to kill the bill. We are also met by another amendment by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McCullough), an amendment which also is meaningless, because it would mean that we amend the Companies Act in a private bill. I will ask you, Mr. Speaker, to declare this second amendment absolutely out of order.
"This bill has been pretty well discussed." That is the hon. member for Selkirk speaking. The C.C.F. group has made its position clear on this bill. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke. If, as the hon. member

subtopic: CONTRIBUTORY SUPERANNUATION SCHEME-COMPENSATION FOR INJURY SUSTAINED IN COURSE OF DUTY
speechtext:
I am glad that at last the government is going to do something by way of superannuation for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Their duties have increased about fourfold owing to the war, and the conditions following it. I am glad to see that the scheme is a contributory one for those members who are at present on the force, if they wish to come in, and for future members.
The minister has added on some of the ordinary provisions which superannuation schemes of civilian police forces throughout the country have had in the past. We have, in connection with our Toronto police force, a contributory system under which the members of the force pay in seven per cent of the fund. But that did not provide for those constables who might be injured in the discharge of their duties, or for widows and orphans.
I am pleased to see that the proposed superannuation scheme is a contributory one; it should not be any other way. It is also pleasing to note that it makes provision for those extra emergencies as will be found in the systems of superannuation in municipal police forces of the country-injuries while on duty, and widows and orphans.
There is one other matter in this connection about which I should like to speak. As I said, the rate used to be seven per cent for the Toronto police force. Then an actuarial report was made by Mr. N. A. Mackenzie, an economist; and he found that, owing to the large number who would be superannuated, the fund would become insolvent. For that reason the city of Toronto had to make provision for the sum of $40,000 over a period of ten years to make it solvent.
It might be said that, since this involves an arrangement between employer and employees, this system might be placed under the Workmen's Compensation Act. However, that could not be done because, like some other public

bodies, including public utilities, they had to qualify under the Workmen's Compensation Act, and under the heading of employers and employees. It will be recalled that that act also operates on a contributory basis, and the contributions have reached a very large sum. The more employees and employers contribute, the better for the fund and for the economic condition of that fund.
I admit that a scheme of that kind could not be applied to the mounted police. They are performing a duty which does credit to the minister and his department. Their work has been greatly intensified in the years since the war, and it must be a heavy burden upon the Department of Justice. However, the force is attracting an even better type of men, and they are all very good. Those men are doing excellent work and, so far as I can see-and I see quite a few of them-I would say that they are doing good work.
A great part of the work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police today comes under the system which has been in operation since confederation, a system through which the enforcement of federal law comes under provincial attorneys general. They, in turn, turn it back to the municipalities, and the municipal police systems.
That is a condition which should not obtain. I believe the time is coming when the Minister of Justice will have to give some compensation to the municipalities which are doing a large part of this work. We know that the municipal police systems throughout the country are enforcing federal laws, and they get nothing for it. It is a direct charge on real estate.
I believe the system should be expanded so that the government could grant to the municipal police systems of the various provinces moneys for the services they render. For example, during the war the city of Toronto spent sums of money running into millions of dollars to maintain our police force and in the enforcement of justice, but the Toronto police commission does not get a dollar from any federal authority for the enforcement of federal laws. Yet they had to enforce tens of thousands of orders in council. I believe there were, all told, over
100,000	orders in council during the war. That was a burden placed upon the municipal police systems, so far as enforcement was concerned.
May I compliment the present minister upon the work he has done since taking over the department. It would appear that in this measure we shall at last have something to offer an even better class of men, many of whom are returned soldiers. They and their

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
families will now have some better protection when they meet with banditry across the country, risking their lives in every day of the year. Some provision will be made under the new system for widows and orphans of those men.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
We have before the house an amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue), seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), reading as follows:
That Bill No. 204 be not now read a second time, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should give further consideration to extending the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to other specialized crop areas, also that the benefits under the act should be increased, and that steps should be taken toward the making of awards on an individual farm basis.
I have considered the amendment very carefully and have to rule it out of order on two grounds. First, I would call the attention of hon. members to citation 551 of Beauchesne, second edition, which reads:
It is a fundamental principle that no resolution or amendment to increase a charge upon the people can be moved with the Speaker in the chair; it must be initiated in committee by a minister acting on behalf of the crown.
I would also call attention to citation 760 which reads:
The principle of relevancy in an amendment governs every proposed resolution, which must, therefore, "strictly relate to the bill which the house, by its order, has resolved upon considering" and must not include in its scope other bills then standing for consideration by the house. Nor may such an amendment deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it ;s moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee, nor attach conditions to the second reading of the bill.
For those two considerations 1 declare the amendment out of order.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before
the house is to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. As has been stated by a number of members, this act was placed upon the statute books in 1939 for the purpose of taking care of conditions that had developed in an area of western Canada subject to drought. The proposal has been made by some hon. members that there should be a zoning of the three western provinces in order that different payments and different collections might be made in different areas.
I would point out that when the bill was first drafted and passed by this house in the
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

form of the present act that question was fully discussed. One of the reasons it was not thought possible to zone successfully and to the advantage of the farmers was the very point made by a number of members. I think this was emphasized more by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) than by the others.
The suggestion was made that the problem which exists could be taken care of by insurance. The hon. member for Lake Centre and others questioned that on the ground that under no plan of insurance could one raise sufficient funds on an actuarial basis to take care of the losses which would occur in the drought areas of western Canada. Because of that fact, it was thought wise that the basis upon which funds would be obtained to take care of the losses ought to be as broad as possible.
In other words, it was felt that there should not be any zoning in order to obtain funds, that the basis should be the whole of Canada, not the province of Manitoba or the province of Saskatchewan or the province of Alberta. It was felt that the only way in which to get sufficient funds to take care of losses which might occur through drought in western Canada was to collect money at the expense of all Canada. I only need to hold up a map of each province showing what has occurred this year in order to indicate why that is true.
This is a map of Manitoba showing the condition in 1947. The red areas are those having under four bushels per acre and the blue areas are those having under eight bushels but more than four bushels per acre. The areas affected are this block in the Dauphin area, this block in the Red river area and this block in the western area. It does not show up as much on this map as it does on the others because the areas affected in Manitoba are not large.
This is a map of Saskatchewan showing the areas affected by drought this year. We hear very little in other parts of Canada about drought this year out west, but if hon. members will look at this map, they can see that the greater part of the province is affected. A considerable part is under four bushels to the acre with a larger part being under eight bushels.
Taking the map of the province of Alberta while the area is not large one must remember that the agricultural areas of the other provinces are not as large as that of the province of Saskatchewan. However, you can see all down the east side of Alberta up north and west of Edmonton is affected. These are maps for this year only.

I repeat, we are not hearing very much with regard to the difficulties that the farmers in western Canada are experiencing as a result of drought. I indicate these areas which are affected only to point out that if you are to take care of areas like that by any means of assistance, the area against which you are going to levy the collection must be a very large area. So we said: We will take one per cent on all the grain delivered in the prairie provinces. That is the first source from which we get funds. Then we provided that in addition to that, we would take all the money that is necessary in order to make up the amount that is to be paid from all the taxpayers in Canada. In other words we take the very broadest basis that can be taken for the collection, and then we make the payments in the areas that are affected by drought. So I suggest that it would not be wise to narrow in any way the basis on which the amounts are levied.
Someone has suggested that this is somewhat similar to unemployment insurance. It is in this sense that a certain amount is paid by the treasury. Someone has suggested that if we paid 50 per cent of the amount into the fund we could administer it on an insurance basis. On the basis on which we have been operating, we have paid out of the federal treasury two-thirds of the amount, and the other one-third has been collected at the rate of one per cent on all the grain delivered. Under unemployment insurance the government pays 20 per cent into the fund, the employer 40 per cent and the employee 40 per cent. But under this prairie farm assistance plan as it has worked out, the government is paying about 66| per cent and the farmers, not only the farmers who may obtain benefits under it but all the farmers in that area, are paying the other one-third under compulsion.
I do not think it would be wise, at any rate at this stage, even to attempt to put it on an insurance basis, even if the federal government had the authority to do so. But rve have always been informed, ever since this legislation was first considered, that it would bo ultra vires of the authority of this parliament to pass legislation providing for insurance in connection with losses of this kind. For that reason, if we were to adopt the insurance plan, it would have to go back to the provinces, and for the reasons I have given only one of the provinces, namely Manitoba, would have a chance of surviving under such an insurance plan. The other two provinces, under no system of assistance that could be given on an insurance basis, could survive.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
If we needed any further proof of that we have only to remember that, following the advice we have received back over the years that only the provinces can bring in an insurance plan in connection with crops, we have had provincial schemes in connection with hail insurance. The losses from hail are not anything like the losses from drought; yet, in spite of that, every one of these provincial schemes has run into difficulties in financing m a provincial basis and some have given it .ip altogether, leaving the insurance to go oack to private companies. So I would suggest to those who are urging that this should be put on a basis of insurance that the area from which you could collect for it would be altogether too small, even if you applied it to all of western Canada.
Some say, Why should we spread the collection over other parts of Canada? I remember the arguments in 1939 with which the house agreed, and some of those arguments have been heard in this house on a number of occasions during recent days in discussing .mother matter. It is generally acknowledged throughout Canada that the great development we have had in this country from about 1890 onwards was due to the railway development in this country and its association with the opening up of western Canada. I think it is generally agreed in all parts of Canada that we could not have had the great industrial development we have had, and certainly we could1 not have maintained our railway organizations on the standard on which they have been maintained, had it not been for the production of the area with which we are concerned when dealing with prairie farm assistance.
One other point ought to be made. When we were discussing this question in 1939 the idea that was in the minds of many people in Canada was that the area which we were talking about had been proven to be nonproductive. Some people even went so far as to say We ought to move out of that area the one million people who had settled in it. Well, we did not do so. Since then, we have gone through the war, and during the period from 1939 down to the present we shall have paid into that area under the scheme by the end of this year S90.000.000. Of that amount we shall have collected 830,000.000 from the fanners in western Canada and we shall have paid out of the treasury of Canada approximately $60,000,000.

speechtext: In all the area pictured on the maps that I held up. What I want to say about that area is this. While we might have thought it had served its purpose so far as producing food products is concerned, nevertheless during the war we have taken more tonnage by a very considerable amount out of that area in the six years of the war than was ever taken out before in a six-year period. In the years when we were breaking up the new prairie and seeding it to cereal crops we no doubt surprised all people living outside western Canada with the production of that area. Then we ran into the drought period from 1930 to 1937, and many people outside that area had the idea that we were through producing in that area. But, as a matter of fact, from 1939 down to the present we have produced more in the area that is known as the drought area in western Canada than was ever produced in it in a corresponding period since it was first broken up. In other words, it is a case of our keeping people in that area and teaching them how to live and how to handle their land to the best advantage, and if that is done over one or two generations they will know how to live there and will be able to produce enough to keep a greater population in the area.

speechtext: Has the minister figures to indicate the production since 1939?

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
I have not them here at the moment; I could give them fairly closely, but I think it is generally acknowledged by all members of the house that the production is very much higher in the area. The reason, then, for continuing this act and for extending it to some extent is the fact that the area is productive; and the reason why all the people in Canada have been willing to pay toward the maintenance of the scheme is that shipments of food out of that area have supplied employment and food for people not only all over Canada but in other parts of the world, and during the war it was the source from which much of the surplus food came that made it possible for us to maintain our armies overseas. I think that is all I need to say with regard to that question.
There are a number of matters which have been brought up by hon. members with regard to which I should say a little. Some have said that we should base the decision as to whether we are to pay on a smaller area. I am surprised to find that many of those
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

dealing with this question still talk about wheat and so many bushels per acre as though they were the main consideration. That is not the consideration at all under this act. We do not care whether the people grow wheat or whether they run cattle. We are not concerned whether they grow feed grain or flax or what they may grow. We use wheat only as a barometer to tell whether it has been dry weather in the area or not, and we believe that wheat yield proves -whether it has been dry or not better than any other crop that is grown, and it is grown more generally over the area. Therefore we say that if the farmer has not produced more than four bushels to the acre on an average, it is proof that it has been dry. Whether he has been running cattle or no matter what he had been doing, he is entitled to payment. We say further that, even if there is a farmer in the district-and this is one of the reasons why I am not in favour of dealing with individuals-who had twenty or twenty-five bushels to the acre on a piece of good summer-fallow of, ilet us say fifty or one hundred acres, and his neighbours or the people all around the area have had an average of four bushels or less per acre or eight bushels or less per acre, that is no reason why the man who has twenty or twenty-five bushels should not be paid. You would have to go into his books and find out everything that he did. whether he produced cattle on grass that had dried out during the season, whether he was feeding hogs for which he did not grow feed grain and a great many other things that have to be examined into before you could say that one fellow was entitled to payment and the other was not.
All we examine into is the question whether in a considerable area it was dry. We say that if the average crop over that area was four bushels or less per acre, then there is a crop failure. If it is eight bushels or less per acre, then it has been dry enough that some assistance ought to be given when the price of wheat is over eighty cents a bushel, and if the price of wheat is lower than eighty cents a bushel, then some assistance should be given up until the yield is twelve bushels to the acre in the area.
Some have said that you could get it down to a section or down to three sections, or you could get it down to four or five farms or half a dozen farms. Those who understand conditions out west know this, and even men in eastern Canada know this, that you can find areas in any country or in any township where you would have three or four farmers on light land. For example, you could go outside Ottawa on the way to the airport and find 
land that used to be occupied by farmers which is now a sand pit. You could find areas like that all over the country. To say that because three or four men insist on living on an area that is nothing more than a- gravel pit or a sand pit and try to farm there, they ought to be maintained there, is not in accordance with the principles of this bill as it is drawn up. We say to these men, We are prepared under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to move you off that land; we will help you pull down your buildings; we wall pay the freight to ship them somewhere else; we will provide you with land in an irrigated district at a certain rate; we will move your equipment there for you. If, after they have had that offer, they will not accept it and still insist on remaining on poor land we say that this act should not provide for that small group of men, within a township that is not eligible, having assistance. Therefore we do not feel that it would be wise to undertake to do it on a smaller district than it now is.
The suggestion has been made that we ought to lower the area from a township to a quarter of a township. In effect, that is what we have already done. We say that wherever there is a block of land of a township or more that is eligible under this act we shall make payment; but we say that if there is a quarter of a township or more that, when we check up, we find has more than fourteen bushels to the acre we can take it out, and we will say that if, around the edge of that block, there is an area that is under eight bushels to the acre we can put it in. In other words, there is not any necessity for dealing with anything less than a whole township in the solid block.
But when you are dealing with the area that I have described in the province of Saskatchewan, the great block which I have shown on the map, every section of land in it is under the act for payment. All that the bill permits us to do is to say that we do not have to go over that whole area and look into the production of every quarter of a township and take one quarter township out and put another quarter township in; when we are satisfied that the average in each township is below the eight bushels to the acre we make payment. The only place that there is any reason for giving consideration to the quarter townships is around the outside of the solid block.
Under this legislation, one of the sections we are amending is the one which has to do with the matter of taking out quarters of townships or putting in quarters of townships, and all the operation takes place around the edge of the solid block which is all in. I say, in effect, that that does put you in the posi-

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
tion that, wherever there is any question about it at all, it is on the nine sections or quarter township basis, and I do not think it is necessary to go below that in order to make units which would meet the wishes of hon. members.
Someone has said that the deductions and payments are the same

I think it was the hon. member for Wood Mountain-

Yes, they are approximately the same. The deductions and payments remain approximately the same as in. 1939 when the act was drawn. The suggestion is made that payments and deductions should go up and down with the variations in the prices of grain. Again I would call the attention of the house to the fact that we are not paying on grain. We are paying on cattle; we are	paying on feed	grain	for	hogs. Weare not	paying on wheat; we	are	paying onanything which a man happens to be doing in the area. He can in relation to agriculture	get payment	even	if	he doesnot sow a bushel of	wheat	or	if he has
not an acre of wheat during the whole period. AVe are paying him because of the condition through which he is going, and that condition affects him no matter what he is trying to produce. Therefore it will not be possible to vary it on the basis of wheat. But even if we attempted to vary it on the basis of the prices for farm products in general, I do not think we would be accomplishing what, we had in mind when we passed the act.
My reason for that is that when you have only four bushels of wheat to the acre and the price is $1 a bushel, your return is only S4 an acre and you need whatever payment there may be more at that time than you need it when wheat is worth $2 a bushel and instead of 14 an acre you get $8. In other words, it would not be fair to the man you are dealing with if you increased the payment he is to get, or even if you increased the amount, he is to pay in. over the period when prices are high. What we are desirous of doing under this bill is accumulating surpluses when prices are high, which make it possible to take care of your people on an equal basis when prices are low.
Up to the present our experience has been that we are faring a little better under this act than we anticipated in 1939. At that time, when we were first getting this measure through, I was asked in the house how much I expected it- would cost the treasury, and I think at that time I said our estimate was that it would cost the fund about $4 for 5849-209J
each SI put up by the farmers. Well, it has worked out that it is costing about $3 for every $1 put up by the farmers; and the only reason we have been able to keep it down to S3 is that in 1942 we did not need to pay out anything. That year there were only twelve townships in all western Canada that had less than eight bushels to the acre, so that no payments were made and everything collected that year was accumulated, to be charged up in the other years.
At the present time, when we have high prices for grain, one per cent means a great deal. But I would suggest to hon. members from Manitoba that in only two years has that one per cent meant enough to cover what Manitoba drew out of the fund the first year. That year Manitoba drew out- $849,000, and the highest collection ever made in Manitoba was $889,000, and in another year, $859,000. I think the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) are quite right in suggesting that Manitoba could have a year like that again. It could have a year twice as bad, because it did have years twice as bad before any such assistance was given, and we could run into that condition again. So that., while they are paying in more than they are getting out for the time being, a time might easily come when they would greatly benefit by the plan.
Perhaps I should say more than I have said already with respect to the meeting that may be held as between the municipalities, the provinces and ourselves with regard to the areas. I think I know what hon. members have in mind when they suggest that we ought to put this plan on an individual basis. They have in mind that group of people who are in the corners. They say that showers do not go in squares; that they simply go across the country, and that when you cut this out in squares you leave the odd corner where a few people live who are just as badly off as the people living inside the solid block. AVe have always acknowledged that; we have always said that is true, but we have called attention to the fact that this was first considered to be a municipal problem. The municipalities were supposed to look after indigent people, just as they were supposed to look after unemployed people and those who are in difficulties for other reasons. AVhen that task became too great for the municipalities, under our constitution the province had to assume the responsibility, and kept on assuming it until it became so big they could not take care of it any longer. Then they came to Ottawa and said, these people are going to
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

starve unless somebody takes care of them; and we entered upon the task.
The basis on which we entered into it was this. We said that when there were twenty-five municipalities in a province which could not take care of themselves, then the dominion government would consider going in and helping. But we said that when the number gets down to ten we shall get out. We were operating on that basis prior to 1939. In that year we said that we would take as our obligation any full townships in the three provinces that were in difficulties, but we suggested that the provinces, or the provinces and the municipalities combined, ought to take care of these corners.
We went along in that way for two or three years. Then we found that they were not going to do anything about it, so we took in quarter townships around the edge. But we said that we would take on quarter townships only on the condition that we were allowed to take out the quarter townships which did not need assistance and which also were around the edge. That is what we have done from that time up to the present. But many people are living in these corners all the way around each block who, as I indicated a moment ago, are not getting assistance under this plan. Every year we have suggested to the government of the province-it did not matter what government it was-that we thought they should go in and pay something toward the care of these people if they wanted us to look after them. If they can provide a scheme of their own to take care of them we are quite satisfied; but we think, if they wish them brought into our plan, the province should contribute.
Now, for the first time, they have all got together in these meetings which were spoken of today, and agreed that we ought to meet to consider this matter. So I would suggest to those who have said we ought to do some things which are not in the amending bill at the present time, that in my opinion the best place for these matters to be discussed is at this meeting which we shall arrange by some method or another, just as soon as we can get away from this house and from some other activities. We shall have a meeting called somewhere, I hope out in western Canada, where we can discuss this question through to a final conclusion; and when we have done so I hope the provinces and municipalities will be able to make some provision by which we can take care of most of the cases that have been discussed here, particularly such cases as were referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), having to

do with blocks on one side of the Qu'Appelle river, when the greater part of the municipality is either down in the valley or extends up the opposite side where the crops are fairly good.
These problems can be taken care of under a plan that may be worked out. Whether the provinces will want to administer the small areas under some plan they will provide, I do not know. We have always said we would be quite satisfied to carry on the administration over the whole area, provided that the provinces, or the provinces plus the municipalities, would put into the fund some amount bearing a reasonable relationship to the amount all the taxpayers of Canada were contributing, in order to deal with the solid block of people who are suffering from drought.
That, I think, is all I need to say at this time.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Well, I do not know. I think I know what my hon. friend has in mind. This bill was not drafted in the first instance to take care of anything but drought, and we have been making payments under the provisions of the act for other reasons. We have been making payments, however, where the destruction that has taken place has covered a township, whether it is by hail or by flooding. Every member of this house knows that ordinarily, w'hen flooding takes place, the responsibility for assistance is with the province. We had very heavy storms in western Ontario, and an appeal was made to us for assistance. We said. No; that was a provincial responsibility. A year or two ago we had the same thing in Quebec, and we said that was a provincial responsibility. We had the same thing up in northern Alberta, and we said that was a provincial responsibility, until finally they showed us that under this act we had authority to pay on full townships.
This year it has been shown in the province of Manitoba that up in the Dauphin area there are additional townships that are affected by flooding. But we still maintain that the responsibility for flooding, generally speaking, is a provincial responsibility, and that the province ought to show some interest in the matter and some inclination to work out a solution for any problem that exists. As the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) will remember, he and I attended a meeting in Dauphin last summer when all this matter was discussed with officials of the province there

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
and with the officials of the municipality. I think we finally reached an understanding that a plan ought to be worked out by the province and submitted to the federal government, and that the federal government might, under the item providing $100,000 we had voted last session, find funds with which to assist in dealing with the problem there.
We did not have a plan working last summer, with the result that the suggestion is made by the hon. member for that area that he would like to have anything that is done made retroactive. I would call his attention to the fact that anything that is done, in addition to what has already been done, would have to be financed by the province. That is, we are taking care of the full township plots, and we would expect that if anything were done beyond that in that area-at least anything beyond the nine sections that might be around the edge of it-it ought to be taken care of out of funds provided by the province. So I am not in a position to say whether it should be retroactive or not.
But I would say that the most important thing for the Dauphin district is not the application of this act at all. The most important thing for the Dauphin district is to do something similar to what we did some years ago in the northeastern corner of Saskatchewan. There is an area there that flooded every spring. The farmers were not able to get on to it until June, and that was too late. The provincial government went into that area and put in drains which drain off the water before it reaches the land, take it down around another way and keep it off that land altogether. I think something of that kind must be done in the Dauphin district, and that is not something which can be handled under this act. It is much more important that we get busy, as soon as possible, with some understanding as between ourselves and the province, and then between the province and the municipality, to have that job done and done in a way that will avoid that flooding. Then the people in that district will not need assistance under this act. and I hope they will not object to paying their one per cent, for all time to come, to take care of the other people.

speechtext:
There is one question that I should like to ask on this first section. The new part reads:
. . . and includes any group of settlement or river lots declared by the governor in council to be a township for the purposes of this act.
The explanatory note says:
This amendment is to provide that the act may apply to areas surveyed as settlement or river lots in the same way as it applies to areas surveyed as townships.
I do not know whether the minister can answer my question tonight, but at all events it will be on the record for the officials. Does this mean that river lots are constituted in a separate block as townships, or is there also the alternative that they may be part of the township? I am just wondering if it leaves out the two alternatives, leaving the discretion to the commission, for instance, to constitute a certain number of river lots into a block or declare it to be a township. Or is the alternative left of leaving them as part of the township.
To illustrate this point, I will give one instance where it would appear that the river lots are taken out entirely. In my constituency there is this year a township, I understand, township 62, which illustrates that point very well. The Red river divides the township north and south practically in the centre. Then there are two rows of river lots on each side of the river. Since it is more or less in the centre of the township, it leaves a strip of sections which are survey sections on the east side and on the west side. My understanding is that the township in question, namely township 6-2-1E, qualifies this year; but, on the other hand, apparently all the river lots in the centre, which are really in this case a part of the township, do not qualify. That is my understanding.
So I do not know if it can be worked out to leave the two alternatives in the act. But I think it would be preferable to leave the two alternatives there; to leave in the intention of the act anyway, the two alternatives open as the case may be required from Jear to year. I do not know if I have made that point clear, but it looks like an anomaly to say that the township qualifies and yet all the strip of land in the very centre does not qualify.

subtopic: AREAS SURVEYED AS SETTLEMENT OR RIVER LOTS- LAND IN ELIGIBLE AND INELIGIBLE TOWNSHIPS
speechtext:
Hon. members who are familiar with the river lots will know that these strips run diagonally as compared with many of the township lots. That is, they were there before the western part of Canada was surveyed into townships six miles square. They
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

ran back from the river at right angles to the river, to begin with; and these strips were formed on both sides of the original. We started out, as a result of the undertaking given last year, to try to draw in what would have been the township boundaries if the survey had been made after the river lots had been put there, to try to make them coincide as nearly as possible with where the lines would have been. The river lots are so much on an angle to where those straight lines would be that this was found to be impossible. If we could have done this, we would simply have drawn a map, made it a schedule to this bill, brought, it in and said: Those are the townships. and any one of those areas must have less than four or eight bushels to the acre before they are paid a certain amount. But we found that it was impossible to do that, so we are taking authority here to go into those districts and layr out areas which are, to all intents and purposes, the same in area as a full township.
It will be found, just as has been indicated by the hon. member, that there may be a township where a piece has been taken out of the middle of it or of the side of it. That is, all over western Canada there are partial townships, and we have another section in this act which is intended to deal with those partial townships.
The legal township is six miles square, but when they come to the next meridian, because the lines you draw toward the north pole come together, eventually there is a correction on these meridians. Those corrections ''ary all the way from six-mile square blocks to blocks which are six miles north and south, but only part of a section or part of a mile east and west.
In this bill we are making provision for dividing these for the purpose of making payments. In other words, while they are not six miles square, they are legal townships. Just alongside these strips of land which run diagonally out from the river, there may be a part of a township which is left, and under the bill they will be designated as separate townships. And these areas which are in the river lots will be separate townships.
I am not altogether certain that there will not be some places where it will be found possible to take what is part of a township and include in it some of the river lots in order to make a complete township for the purposes of this act. But eventually the map will be drawn and it will be properly made out. so that we are not deciding the matter until after the facts are known. The boundaries will be there before. Then, when the

facts develop which make it possible to pay under the act, we shall pay under the act.

speechtext:
Well, I think I remember informing the house at that time as to the regulations. The regulations, as they were drawn in the first instance, including this 20-mile limit, and all that kind of thing, were discussed on the floor of the house.
One of the reasons it has been found difficult to cover what is in the regulations by law lias been the fact that we are receiving continuously representations from members and others indicating the difficulties people get into.
Take, for instance the question of widowed mothers having to move into towns and leaving their land. Sometimes they move a little more than twenty miles, or they may have moved into a town more than twenty miles away in order to obtain hospitalization. That question was brought up. If we had been committed to twenty miles by the legislation, we could not have done anything. But having the authority to amend the regulations, we were able to say, Well, in cases where people have gone to hospitals and had to go more than twenty miles, and where they have had to remain there for a period of time-sometimes two or three years- for treatment of different types of diseases, payments can be made.
It is to meet a situation of that kind that authority has been left to have regulations made by orders in council. I am not able to make them myself. The board cannot make them. But the whole council can change those regulations from time to time.
Another case was that of soldiers. During the war soldiers just picked up from their

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
land, enlisted and went overseas. They did not think anything about prairie farm assistance. Probably they did not know they would have any crop failures while they were away, or at least did not think they would have. But they got overseas. Those people were the owners of land, the real operators of it, although they hired men to look after it.
It was found that, strictly speaking, these men did not have a claim unless we did something about the matter in the regulations. We dealt with those cases and said that when a man was overseas he was an exception. All kinds of cases of that kind have come up, and we have dealt with them. I think hon. members will agree that we have attempted to administer the act so that it would not create undue hardship, and so that it would not give favours to anybody. I believe that is pretty well agreed, because it was so stated many times this afternoon by hon. members.

I was
glad to hear the minister say that the municipal association was meeting with the government with a view to coming to some decision whereby some of these injustices would be 5849-210
ironed out and provision made to take care of them. But here you have in an eligible township, say six sections with a fairly good crop, and in order that the department may take a block of one-quarter of a township it includes three more sections where the farmers have poor crops. Those farmers do not feel that they should be included in any sort of relief system administered either by the municipality or by the provincial government, nor would it be reasonable to expect that, when they are suffering crop losses for the very same reason as these other people and they get no award under the act. We could amend this section in a way that would ensure that the farmers who had suffered crop losses would be paid something, without in any way increasing the expenditure of the government, and so I move, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn:
That section 3 of Bill 204 be amended by deleting all the words in lines 5 to 11, both inclusive, thereof, and substituting therefor the following:
"(a) where any farm is located in a township contiguous to an eligible township, it shall be eligible for award; but no farm which has an average yield of more than fourteen bushels of wheat per acre, no matter where it is located, shall be eligible for award."
This does not in any way penalize any farmer who should get an award, but it reduces the expenditure of the government through not paying any award to a farmer who, I think, should not get an award because he has a decent crop, namely, fourteen bushels to the acre. I think that is only reasonable.

That is again the idea that we are paying on wheat. We are not paying on wheat at all.
I do not know the Acadia area very well, but I have been over it a number of times. As the hon. member will admit, I think it is one of the most difficult areas in either Alberta or western Saskatchewan, and I know that people there are experiencing considerable hardship, and will until certain things can be done which have not been done and may not be done for a long time. But I do not think you can take care of all these difficulties by any rule-of-thumb thing that we can put into this act. We simply say that if there is an area there that has an average of dess than

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
four bushels to the acre they are entitled to $2.50 an acre. If we say it is under eight bushels to the acre they are entitled to SI.50 an acre.
To say that you would have to find an area that has not anybody in it who has twenty bushels to the acre or fourteen bushels to the acre would just make the thing inoperative. You would take out probably half the people who are getting assistance, and it would not be just to them to take them out. On the other hand, if you said that every fellow who has under four bushels to the acre is to get paid no matter what he does, some fellows would sit in the house probably and wait for their $4 an acre and do better than if they worked, particularly if they are living on a piece of sandy land. My hon. friend knows there is land of that kind in the area about which he is talking. If a man insists on living on that sandy land and says that he can live there and get $4 an acre by living there, I do not think we should help him to do that. Some people could have activities elsewhere of a kind that makes it possible for them to live there. I do not think we should do either one thing or the other. I do not think we should shut the man out who may have twenty bushels to the acre on a very limited acreage of wheat but who may be trying to feed a hundred head of cattle for which he has no grass, and at the same time take another fellow in who just insists on living on a piece of land whether he can ever grow more than four bushels to the acre or not. I believe this is a very useful act, but I do not think it should be considered separately but rather as part of the whole program for agriculture. We have two other acts that have done a great deal for the western provinces, the P.F.R.A. and the wheat board act. We are beginning to eliminate the risks and provide ourselves with safeguards against emergencies. In effect, the long-term contracts are price insurance. The P.F.R.A. has helped us to insure a water supply. The dugouts all over the west have been a tremendous help in maintaining the livestock population, and under the P.F.R.A. we have taken a great deal of submarginal land out of production.
These things when integrated could work into a stabilization of our whole agricultural industry and help maintain a high level of prosperity and spending which would be a great aid to Canada's whole economy. I suggest to the minister that we extend this program to include the principle of insurance. I was interested the other evening to hear the Minister of Reconstruction outline the provisions of the amendments to the Export Credits Insurance Act. As reported at page 2774 of Hansard he said:
More than seventy different countries received a variety of agricultural products, raw materials, and manufactured goods from Canadian exporters, insured by the corporation.
Under that act we insure against such things as war, revolution and defaulting governjnents. If we can insure our exporters against risks of that kind, which include such tremendous upheavals as war and revolution; if we can insure our agricultural products when they reach the export stage, surely we can work out a system of crop insurance on the first level to cover the man who is actually in the business of producing. I do not think we should consider it too expensive a proposition to put on an actuarial basis. It would not be nearly as expensive as the loss of a crop is to an individual. Speaking as a farmer, I would much rather put in five or six bushels or more, when I had the bushels, than lose an entire crop and have nothing but the very small payment now being made under this act. I think it is only intelligent to put it on the basis of insurance and remove it from the category of relief, because it was originated with the idea of helping the farmers set up a system to pay for each other's relief and thus take us off the federal treasury.
I am' glad the minister made a statement a few minutes ago as to the amount the government has put in. I do not think it is too much when one considers the contribution agriculture makes in this country, and the sacrifices agriculture has made in accepting lower prices when we might have had higher prices.
I think we have accepted the principle of insurance. We have unemployment insurance; we are considering health insurance, and we are also considering a contributory old age pension scheme. This may be slightly off the subject, but I think it is part of the argument. A contributory old age pension will be insurance against old age, and I think it is not too much to ask that we should begin now to put agriculture on an insurance basis, so that in years of crop failure we shall have more than a relief standard.

I dealt fully with that question. If the hon. member will read Hansard, he will find that is so. It constituted most of the speech I made. I pointed out that the matter of making it possible to pay under this bill necessitated the widest base possible from which collections are to be made, and we have made that base the whole Dominion of Canada. In so far as the farmer himself is concerned, we have made the basis all the farmers in the west. Just as the hon. member for Souris pointed out, if you tried to make it any higher, and districts that are never going to collect would raise some objection, and naturally so. As long as you keep it to one per cent, they say: All right, we will go along with you. But when we start to make it five or six per cent, or get it up to twenty per cent or sixteen per cent which is necessary to carry it in the areas that are affected, we would run into trouble.
I cannot argue that question of insurance, because, when this bill was drafted, I was definitely told by every legal authority we are advised by, that we just cannot pass insurance legislation on a question of this kind. I took the matter into the senate. I was asked to go there myself. Mr. Meighen was the leader of the opposition in the senate, and the legal adviser to the senate was there. Mr. Meighen asked him the definite question. He said: Is this insurance? The legal adviser said that, in his opinion, it was not, and because of that he thought it was intra vires. It was on the strength of that advice that it got through the committee over in the senate, and finally through the senate itself and came back here. I am absolutely convinced from all I have had to do with it that we cannot bring in crop insurance.
The only other thing I can say about it is that for fifty years 'to my knowledge 'the farmers in western Canada asked for crop insurance; or rather for forty years up to about ten years ago, they asked for crop insurance and never were able to get it. When I came here I made up my mind that we would not talk about crop insurance but would talk about prairie farm assistance, and we got that inside of two years. I would rather take what we obtained after two years of discussion of

something which can be given, than to go back and start talking about something which we talked about for forty years and could not get. I do not want to go back and talk about that.
